supplementary_info.identification_information: 60-80 cm. Male is a slender grey pheasant with an irridescent green (can appear black) tail. Long red legs and facial skin. Prominent coronal tuft. Female lacks crest, has a rufous mantle and underparts and banded wings and tail. Similar spp. none if seen well.

documentation.range: This species is found in Thailand in the north-east and south-east), Lao PDR, Cambodia and Viet Nam; at least historically, also occurred in eastern Myanmar.
documentation.population: The population size has not been robustly estimated, but it is described as 'uncommon to fairly common' in Thailand (Treesucon and Limparungpatthanakij 2018), 'scarce' in south-west and north-west Cambodia (CBGA 2019), 'locally fairly common' in north and north-east Cambodia (CBGA 2019) and is locally common in Lao PDR, which may support the largest national population (Thewlis et al. 1998, Brickle et al. 2008, Timmins et al. 2024). At one site in Thailand, the density of Siamese Firebacks was calculated as 5.6 birds km2 in dry evergreen forest, but only 0.2 birds/km2 in old forest plantations (Suwanrat et al. 2015). Extrapolating these densities from Thailand across the species' range is challenging owing to significant variation in hunting intensity (which is typically much higher in all other range states), however it is likely that the global population probably numbers in the tens of thousands.
documentation.habitats: It occurs in evergreen, semi-evergreen and bamboo forest, secondary growth and scrub, often near roads and tracks through the forest, chiefly in the plains and foothills to 300 m, but occasionally up to 800 m, and exceptionally 1,150 m. It seems able to tolerate considerable degradation of its forest habitat (Thewlis et al. 1998, Brickle et al. 2008) but may become extirpated from small, isolated fragments (Timmins et al. 2024). Occurrence in plantations appears to be marginal (Suwanrat et al. 2015). The species occurs in small groups which are presumed to be family parties.
documentation.threats: This species is threatened by continuing extensive lowland forest destruction within its range and, perhaps more severely, by hunting and snaring. However throughout its range it is resistant to habitat degradation and is able to tolerate intense hunting pressures, though less so snaring (Brickle et al. 2008, Timmins et al. 2024). Nonetheless, the rate of forest cover loss, caused by forest clearance and conversion to plantations, is rapid enough that it is highly likely now to be driving moderately rapid declines (Global Forest Watch 2025). Moreover, hunting (particularly that done with snares) is probably compounding declines, and there is evidence the species has disappeared from fragmented, accessible forest patches (Timmins et al. 2024). In Lao PDR, forest is being lost through conversion to plantations of Eucalyptus, Acacia, rubber, fruiting trees and cassava, for example; in Thailand, there is evidence the species occurs in plantations at a much lower density than in native forest (Suwanrat et al. 2015).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions Underway
The species occurs in a number of protected areas, however they often provide only limited protection against hunting and logging activities (S. Mahood in litt. 2011, F. Goes in litt. 2011).

Conservation Actions Proposed
Increase the existing protected area network. Support governments in their efforts to control illegal logging in South-East Asia. Determine the current global population size and trend. Support efforts to tackle the issue of hunting inside protected areas.
documentation.use_trade: Regularly hunted in its range, particularly in Lao PDR, Viet Nam and Cambodia (Thewlis et al. 1998, Brickle et al. 2008, Timmins et al. 2024); remarkably resistant to hunting pressure, with densities barely any lower in heavily hunted forest patches in Lao PDR (Brickle et al. 2008). However, it is less resistant to intensive snaring (Timmins et al. 2024) which is a considerable threat in Lao PDR, Viet Nam and Cambodia (see Gray et al. 2018). There is some demand for the species in captivity, but this is considered a negligible threat.
documentation.rationale: Although this species has proven adaptable to forest degradation and some degree of hunting, extensive forest loss compounded by locally industrial scales and intensities of hunting are now likely to be driving moderately rapid rates of population decline. The species now approaches the thresholds for listing as threatened, and is accordingly assessed as Near Threatened.
documentation.trend_justification:
This species is inferred to be declining in response to ongoing forest cover loss and hunting.

Although considered a 'low priority for action' by Brickle et al. (2008) and descriptions in various recent literature mention that it remains locally common or even abundant (e.g. Goes 2013, Treesucon and Limparungpatthanakij 2018, CBGA 2019, Timmins et al. 2024), it is highly likely that Siamese Fireback has declined moderately rapidly over the past three generations (21 years). In this time, forest cover extent in its range has declined by 23-26% (Global Forest Watch 2025, based on data from Hansen et al. 2013). While this species has been recorded in plantations, it occurs in them at much lower densities (Suwanrat et al. 2015) and a considerable amount of forest loss in its range has amounted to total clearfelling for infrastructure and agricultural expansion, leaving no suitable habitat remaining. Thus while the relationship between forest cover loss and population trend may not be entirely linear, the scale of forest loss is thought almost certainly to have driven moderately rapid population declines.

Hunting pressure throughout this species' range is very high (e.g. Harrison et al. 2016) and intensive (and non-discriminatory) snaring is a considerable threat (Gray et al. 2018); while the species has proven itself remarkably tolerant of even intensive hunting pressure (e.g. Brickle et al. 2008, Timmins et al. 2024 and references therein), it is less tolerant of intensive snaring, and in Lao PDR is reported to 'have been extirpated from easily accessible and fragmented forest areas' (Timmins et al. 2024).

Overall, the species is suspected to have declined at a rate of 15-29% over the past three generations. Future rates of population decline are somewhat uncertain, but recent years have shown a slight acceleration in annual rates of forest cover loss (Global Forest Watch 2025).
